title: Algorithmic Optimization of the Gaussian Sampler in the FN-DSA Post-Quantum Signature Scheme
abstract:
The post-quantum signature scheme Falcon (FN-DSA), currently being standardized by NIST as FIPS 206 (Initial Public Draft submitted August 2025, final standard expected 2026-2027), relies on a discrete Gaussian sampler whose critical bottleneck is the function fpr_expm_p63, computing $\lfloor \exp(-x) \cdot 2^{63} \rfloor$ for $x \in [0, \ln 2)$. While the reference implementation already employs a degree-12 fixed-point polynomial (FACCT), no segmented approximation has been studied for this specific function, nor has empirical timing security been published on ARM Cortex-M3 (emulated or physical).

This paper presents a systematic study of piecewise polynomial approximation applied to fpr_expm_p63, combining the Remez exchange algorithm (computed with 50 decimal digits of precision via mpmath), fixed-point arithmetic, and Horner evaluation. Two configurations are implemented and evaluated: a 32-segment degree-6 approximation at scale $2^{62}$ targeting x86-64, and a 16-segment degree-3 approximation at scale $2^{31}$ (256-byte LUT) targeting ARM Cortex-M3 IoT devices without hardware floating-point unit (FPU).

Against the authentic FACCT reference from Falcon's fpr.c, ported verbatim to ARM Cortex-M3 (emulated via QEMU user-mode with arm-linux-gnueabi -mfloat-abi=soft), our implementation achieves a $1.28\times$ median speedup across 30 independent runs (range $1.24\times$ to $1.33\times$), measured with a rigorous anti-noise protocol combining batch measurement, aggressive warm-up, ref/opt interleaving, and percentile filtering (P5-P95). DUDECT timing leakage tests confirm that both the FACCT reference (t-score $\in [0.05, 2.51]$) and our implementation (t-score $\in [1.99, 5.24]$) remain within statistical safety thresholds in the vast majority of runs (FACCT: 30/30; optimized: 27/30). Static instruction-level analysis via objdump disassembly provides deterministic constant-time evidence: zero data-dependent conditional branches, zero FPU instructions, and zero soft-float calls, yielding a branchless fixed-point Horner core; however, the full constant-time claim is limited to the tested compilation target and memory model.

To the best of our knowledge, this constitutes the first comparative study of segmented versus global polynomial approximation for fpr_expm_p63 in the FN-DSA context, and the first empirical DUDECT measurement of this function on emulated ARM Cortex-M3 against the authentic FACCT reference. Physical hardware validation on STM32F103 is identified as future work.

1    Introduction
The advent of large-scale quantum computers poses a fundamental threat to classical
public-key cryptography. Shor’s algorithm [Sho94] can solve the integer factorization and

discrete logarithm problems in polynomial time, rendering RSA, DSA, and elliptic-curve
cryptography vulnerable. In response, the National Institute of Standards and Technology
(NIST) launched a post-quantum cryptography (PQC) standardization process in 2016,
culminating in the publication of three finalized standards in August 2024: ML-KEM
(FIPS 203), ML-DSA (FIPS 204), and SLH-DSA (FIPS 205). A fourth standard, FN-DSA
(FIPS 206), based on the FALCON signature scheme [FAL20], was submitted as an Initial
Public Draft in August 2025, with finalization expected in 2026–2027.
    FALCON is a hash-then-sign lattice-based signature scheme operating over NTRU
lattices. It offers among the smallest signature sizes and public keys of any post-quantum
signature scheme, making it particularly attractive for constrained environments such as
IoT devices, embedded systems, and smart cards. However, FALCON’s signing procedure
relies on a discrete Gaussian sampler that requires floating-point arithmetic and Fast
Fourier Transform (FFT) computations, making it both computationally intensive and
notoriously difficult to implement securely against side-channel attacks.

1.1     The fpr_expm_p63 Bottleneck
At the core of FALCON’s Gaussian sampler lies the function fpr_expm_p63, which com-
putes:
               fpr_expm_p63(x, ccs) = ccs · exp(−x) · 263 , x ∈ [0, ln 2)
                                                        

This function is called repeatedly by the Bernoulli sampler (BerExp) during each signature
generation, accounting for a significant fraction of the total signing time. The reference
implementation evaluates this function using a degree-12 fixed-point polynomial with
hardcoded uint64_t coefficients derived from the FACCT work [ZSS20]. While this avoids
native floating-point instructions, the implementation contains no published empirical
security analysis, and a comment in the source code explicitly suggests that unsigned
__int128 on GCC/Clang could improve performance.
    In the NIST PQC standardization forum, NIST has explicitly solicited community
input on whether to support a fixed-point version of FN-DSA signing. Respondents raised
concerns about floating-point arithmetic, one noting that “any use of Falcon with an
external floating point implementation seems worrisome” [Nom25]. This concern directly
motivates our work.

1.2     Contributions
This paper makes the following contributions:
    1. Piecewise polynomial approximation of fpr_expm_p63. We propose and
       implement a segmented Remez minimax approximation (computed with 50 decimal
       digits of precision via mpmath) combined with fixed-point Horner evaluation and
       constant-time segment selection via binary masking. Two configurations are provided:
       32 segments of degree 6 at scale 262 for x86-64, and 16 segments of degree 3 at scale
       231 (256-byte LUT) for ARM Cortex-M3.
    2. First empirical DUDECT analysis of fpr_expm_p63 on emulated ARM
       Cortex-M3 against the authentic FACCT reference. Using the DUDECT
       leakage detection methodology [RBV17], we provide the first published timing leakage
       measurement of this function on an ARM architecture without FPU, benchmarked
       against the official FACCT-derived polynomial ported verbatim from Falcon’s fpr.c.
       Across 30 stabilized runs, both the reference (t ∈ [0.05, 2.51]) and our implementation
       (t-score ∈ [1.99, 5.24]) remain within statistical safety thresholds in the vast majority
       of runs (FACCT: 30/30; optimized: 27/30), with residual variance attributed to
       QEMU JIT scheduler noise and confirmed as non-leakage by static instruction-level
       analysis.

    3. Instruction-level constant-time verification. We verify at the machine code level,
       using objdump disassembly (arm-linux-gnueabi-gcc -O1 -fno-inline), that the
       core Horner evaluation loop of our implementation contains zero data-dependent
       conditional branches, zero FPU instructions, and zero soft-float calls. This yields
       a branchless fixed-point Horner core; our full constant-time claim is limited to the
       tested compilation target and memory model. Note that this constitutes static
       instruction-level analysis, distinct from formal verification via theorem provers (e.g.,
       Coq, F*).

    4. IoT performance benchmark on emulated ARM Cortex-M3 against Fal-
       con’s authentic FACCT reference. Cross-compiled with arm-linux-gnueabi-gcc
      -mfloat-abi=soft and executed under QEMU user-mode ARM emulation (not
       physical hardware) with real-time scheduling (chrt -f 99 taskset -c 0), our im-
       plementation achieves a 1.28× median speedup across 30 independent runs (range
       1.24×–1.33×, ±3% variance) against the FACCT polynomial ported verbatim from
       Falcon’s reference fpr.c. The measurement uses a rigorous anti-noise protocol com-
       bining batch measurement (1000 calls per data point), aggressive warm-up (10,000
       iterations), strict ref/opt interleaving, and percentile filtering (P5–P95 on speed
       only, not DUDECT). Precision is ≈ 2−28 using a 256-byte LUT. Physical hardware
       validation on STM32F103 is identified as future work.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows.
    Section 2 reviews FALCON’s Gaussian sampler, the role of fpr_expm_p63, and related
work. Section 3 presents the mathematical framework. Section 4 details the implementation
for both x86-64 and ARM Cortex-M3. Section 5 reports experimental results. Section 6
presents the security analysis. Section 7 discusses limitations and perspectives, and
Section 8 concludes.


2     Background and Related Work
2.1     The FALCON Signature Scheme
FALCON [FAL20] is a lattice-based digital signature scheme built on the hardness of the
Short Integer Solution (SIS) problem over NTRU lattices. It operates in the hash-then-sign
paradigm: given a message m, FALCON first computes a hash t = H(r∥m) where r is
a random salt, then finds a short lattice vector s such that s · H = t (mod q), where H
is derived from the public key. The signature is s, which is short by construction of the
Gaussian sampler.
    FALCON operates over the ring Zq [x]/(xn + 1) with n ∈ {512, 1024} and q = 12289. Its
main advantage over competing schemes (ML-DSA, SLH-DSA) is signature compactness:
Falcon-512 produces signatures of 666 bytes and public keys of 897 bytes, making it
particularly suited for bandwidth-constrained IoT deployments [FAL20].

2.2     The Discrete Gaussian Sampler
The security of FALCON relies critically on the ability to p

to a discrete Gaussian distribution DZ,σ , where σ ≈ 1.17 q/2 is the standard deviation.
An imperfect Gaussian sampler one whose output distribution deviates from the ideal can
leak information about the secret key through statistical analysis of signatures [FAL20].
    FALCON’s signing procedure expands the private key into a Fast Fourier Transform
(FFT) tree and samples using an algorithm based on the Fast Fourier Sampling technique.

2.4    The Reference Implementation
The reference implementation of fpr_expm_p63 in fpr.c [FAL20] evaluates a single global
polynomial of degree 12 over the full interval [0, ln 2), using 13 hardcoded uint64_t
coefficients derived from the FACCT work [ZSS20]:

static const uint64_t C[] = {
    0x00000004741183A3u, /* c_0 */
    0x00000036548CFC06u, /* c_1 */
    ...
    0x8000000000000000u   /* c_12 */
};

    The evaluation uses a manual 32-bit split multiplication to simulate 64-bit×64-bit→128-
bit products, with a comment noting that unsigned __int128 on GCC/Clang could
improve speed. While this implementation avoids FPU instructions, it has never been
subjected to published empirical timing security analysis.


2.5    Side-Channel Attacks on Gaussian Samplers
Timing side-channel attacks on Gaussian samplers represent a well-documented threat in
lattice-based cryptography. An attacker who can measure the execution time of the signing
function may recover statistical information about the secret key if the timing varies with
the input. The DUDECT methodology [RBV17] provides a standard statistical test for
detecting such leakage: it applies a Welch t-test to compare execution time distributions
under fixed versus random inputs, flagging implementations where |t| ≥ 4.5 as potentially
leaky.
    This risk is actively discussed in the NIST PQC standardization forum, where the
possibility of specifying a fixed-point version of FN-DSA signing has been raised for
community feedback [Nom25].

2.6     Related Work
Fixed-point Gaussian sampling. Brannigan [Bra21] proposed applying the Remez al-
gorithm with piecewise splines to evaluate transcendental functions (logarithm, square
root) required by Box-Muller Gaussian samplers, achieving constant-time evaluation via
fixed-point arithmetic. Our work applies a similar mathematical framework to the specific
function fpr_expm_p63 of FN-DSA, which uses a different sampling algorithm (rejection
sampling via BerExp rather than Box-Muller), and provides empirical DUDECT validation
on ARM hardware.

ARM optimizations of Falcon. Choi et al. [CYS25] recently optimized Falcon verification
on ARM Cortex-M4, achieving significant speedups through signed Plantard modular
arithmetic and optimized NTT-based polynomial multiplication. In contrast, our work
targets Falcon signing specifically the fpr_expm_p63 bottleneck on the more constrained
Cortex-M3 architecture without FPU, a configuration that has received no published
analysis.

NCC Group optimization. The NCC Group [Mar19] proposed an assembly-level opti-
mization of fpr_expm_p63 for ARM, reducing branch and memory instructions without
modifying the mathematical structure of the approximation. Our contribution differs
in that we study the segmentation strategy itself, providing a comparative analysis of
piecewise versus global polynomial approximation with empirical security measurements.


3       Mathematical Framework
This section presents the theoretical foundations underlying our piecewise polynomial
approximation of exp(−x). We follow a principled construction: from the existence
guarantee (Weierstrass), through the optimality criterion (Chebyshev equioscillation), to
the practical computation algorithm (Remez), and finally to the constant-time evaluation
scheme (fixed-point Horner with binary masking).

3.2     Minimax Approximation
3.2.1    The Chebyshev Equioscillation Theorem
Among all polynomials of degree d, the one minimizing the supremum norm ∥f − P ∥∞ is
called the minimax (or best uniform) approximation, denoted P ∗ . Its characterization is
given by the following fundamental theorem.
 Nicolas Houlès and Thibaut Heckmann                                                           7


Theorem 2 (Chebyshev Equioscillation, 1853). A polynomial P ∗ ∈ Rd [x] is the best
uniform approximation to f ∈ C([a, b]) if and only if there exist at least d + 2 points
a ≤ x0 < x1 · · · < xd+1 ≤ b such that:
                  f (xk ) − P ∗ (xk ) = (−1)k · λ · ∥f − P ∗ ∥∞ ,   λ ∈ {−1, +1}
These points are called alternation points or equioscillation points.
    The equioscillation condition means that the error f (x) − P ∗ (x) achieves its maximum
absolute value at exactly d + 2 points, alternating in sign. This is both a characterization
and a certificate of optimality: if one can exhibit d + 2 alternation points, the polynomial
is provably optimal.

3.2.2     The Remez Algorithm
The minimax polynomial P ∗ is computed iteratively by the Remez algorithm [Rem34],
which converges to the equioscillation solution:
   1. Initialization. Choose d + 2 initial reference points {x0 , . . . , xd+1 } in [a, b] (e.g.,
      Chebyshev nodes).
   2. Polynomial fit. Solve the linear system:
                            P (xk ) + (−1)k λ = f (xk ),     k = 0, . . . , d + 1
        for the d + 1 polynomial coefficients and the equioscillation error λ.
   3. Error maximization. Find the point x∗ = arg maxx∈[a,b] |f (x) − P (x)|.
   4. Reference update. Replace the reference point in the appropriate interval with
      x∗ , maintaining the alternation property.
   5. Convergence check. If |∥f − P ∥∞ − |λ|| < ε, stop. Otherwise, return to step 2.
    In our implementation, the Remez algorithm is executed in Python using the mpmath
library [Joh23] with 50 decimal digits of precision, ensuring that coefficient quantization
errors remain negligible relative to the approximation error.

3.3      Fixed-Point Representation
3.3.1     Motivation
Native floating-point evaluation of exp(−x) on microcontrollers without FPU requires
software emulation via the ARM EABI soft-float library (__aeabi_dmul, __aeabi_dsub,
etc.), which incurs 200–500 clock cycles per operation and introduces data-dependent
timing variations. Fixed-point arithmetic, by contrast, uses only integer ALU operations
(multiply, shift, add), which execute in constant time on ARM Cortex-M3.

4.2   Coefficient Generation Pipeline
Coefficients are generated offline via a Python script using mpmath [Joh23] at 50 decimal
digits of precision, following four steps:

  1. For each segment i ∈ {0, . . . , k − 1}, sample nfit points uniformly in [ai , bi ] and
     evaluate f (x) = exp(−x) at high precision.
  2. Apply the Remez exchange algorithm on the segment: initialize with d + 2 Chebyshev
     nodes on (ai , bi ), iteratively solve the alternation system and update reference points
     via error maximization on a dense grid, until the equioscillation error λ and the
     empirical supremum error agree within 10−30 (typically 5 iterations on our segments).
  3. Quantize coefficients: ĉj ← round(cj · 2N ).
  4. Verify the quantized polynomial via integer Horner evaluation at nverify = 10,000
     uniformly distributed points, recording the maximum relative error.

    This pipeline is implemented in generate_lut.py (x86-64) and generate_lut_arm.py
(ARM), which export C header files (splines_data.h, lut_arm.h) containing the quan-
tized coefficient tables as static const arrays.

4.3   x86-64 Configuration
The x86-64 implementation targets the FALCON reference codebase compiled natively,
where the type fpr is defined as struct { double v; } (FALCON_FPNATIVE mode). Our
configuration uses:

  • k = 32 segments, degree d = 6, scale N = 62
  • LUT size: 32 × 7 × 8 = 1792 bytes
  • Horner evaluation via __int128 (GCC/Clang extension), with intermediate products
    bounded at 119 of 127 available bits

uint64_t fpr_expm_p63(fpr x, fpr ccs) {
    double xd = x.v, ccsd = ccs.v;
    uint32_t seg = (uint32_t)(xd * INV_SEG_W)
                   & (EXP_N_SEG - 1U);
    double xl = xd - (double)seg * SEG_W;
    __int128 xl_fix =
        (__int128)(xl * 4611686018427387904.0);
                              /* xl * 2^62 */
    const int64_t *c = EXP_LUT[seg];
    __int128 p = (__int128)c[6];
    p = ((p * xl_fix) >> 62) + c[5];
    p = ((p * xl_fix) >> 62) + c[4];
    p = ((p * xl_fix) >> 62) + c[3];
    p = ((p * xl_fix) >> 62) + c[2];
    p = ((p * xl_fix) >> 62) + c[1];
    p = ((p * xl_fix) >> 62) + c[0];
    __int128 ccs_fix =
        (__int128)(ccsd * 4611686018427387904.0);
    __int128 r = ((p * ccs_fix) >> 62) << 1;
    return (uint64_t)r;
}

4.4      ARM Cortex-M3 Configuration
The ARM target requires a distinct configuration because __int128 is not natively available
on 32-bit architectures; GCC emulates it via paired 32-bit registers, incurring significant
overhead. We therefore use:

     • k = 16 segments, degree d = 3, scale N = 31
     • LUT size: 16 × 4 × 4 = 256 bytes
     • Horner evaluation via native int32_t coefficients with int64_t intermediate products
       (natively supported via ARM smull/umull instructions)

static uint64_t opt_expm(double x, double ccs) {
    uint32_t seg = (uint32_t)(x * INV_SEG_W_ARM)
                   & (N_SEG_ARM - 1U);
    double xl = x - seg * SEG_W_ARM;
    int32_t xlf = (int32_t)(xl * 2147483648.0);
                              /* xl * 2^31 */
    int32_t p = LUT_ARM[seg][3];
    p = (int32_t)(((int64_t)p * xlf) >> 31)
        + LUT_ARM[seg][2];
    p = (int32_t)(((int64_t)p * xlf) >> 31)
        + LUT_ARM[seg][1];
    p = (int32_t)(((int64_t)p * xlf) >> 31)
        + LUT_ARM[seg][0];
    int64_t ccs_fix = (int64_t)(ccs * 2147483648.0);
    int64_t r = ((int64_t)p * ccs_fix) << 1;
    return (uint64_t)r;
}

6       Security Analysis
This section evaluates the resistance of both implementations to timing side-channel attacks
through three complementary methods: the DUDECT statistical leakage test, Pearson
correlation analysis, and instruction-level analysis via disassembly. We emphasize that no
single method is individually sufficient; together, they constitute converging evidence of
constant-time behavior.


6.1     Threat Model
We consider an attacker capable of measuring the execution time of fpr_expm_p63 with
fine-grained precision (e.g., via a local timing oracle or shared microarchitectural resources).
The attacker’s goal is to recover information about the secret key by observing whether
execution time correlates with the (secret-dependent) input value x. This is the standard
threat model for timing side-channel analysis of cryptographic primitives [RBV17].

7     Discussion and Limitations
This section discusses the limitations of our experimental methodology and identifies
directions for future work, following the principle that transparent acknowledgment of
limitations strengthens rather than weakens the validity of empirical claims.

7.1     QEMU Emulation versus Physical Hardware
All ARM Cortex-M3 results in this paper were obtained via QEMU user-mode emulation
(qemu-arm) running on an x86-64 host, rather than on physical hardware. While the
-mfloat-abi=soft compilation flag faithfully reproduces the instruction-level absence of
FPU hardware verified directly via disassembly (Section 6.4) several properties of real
hardware are not captured by this emulation:

    • Clock frequency. QEMU executes at host CPU speed (multi-GHz x86-64) rather
      than the target 72 MHz Cortex-M3 clock, making absolute timing values non-
      representative; even relative speedup ratios are only indicative, as discussed in
      Section 5.6.

    • Memory hierarchy. Physical Cortex-M0/M3 microcontrollers typically lack data
      caches, meaning LUT accesses incur uniform flash wait-state latency. On the QEMU
      host, LUT accesses benefit from x86 cache hierarchy, potentially understating the
      relative cost of memory access in our approach compared to register- only computation
      in the reference implementation.

    • Pipeline behavior. ARM Cortex-M3 uses a simple 3-stage in-order pipeline,
      while the QEMU host executes translated instructions on a deeply out-of-order
      x86-64 pipeline, affecting the relative cost of branches and memory operations. This
      limitation is explicitly noted by Markelon [Mar19], who observes that qemu-arm
      targets Linux binaries on A-profile cores rather than simulating an M-profile core.

    • Scheduling noise. As discussed in Section 6, QEMU’s just-in-time binary transla-
      tion introduces non-deterministic timing variance attributable to the host operating
      system scheduler, requiring real-time priority control (chrt/taskset) to obtain

7.2    Residual Soft-Float Calls and Constant-Time Scope
Disassembly analysis (Section 6.4) confirms that the core Horner evaluation loop of
opt_expm contains zero data-dependent branches, zero FPU instructions, and zero soft-float
calls. However, the surrounding argument-reduction steps (computing x · INV_SEG_W
and x − seg · SEG_W on double inputs) invoke the ARM EABI soft-float routines
__aeabi_dmul and __aeabi_dsub.
    Critically, we caution that these routines are not guaranteed to be constant-time. Dis-
assembly of __aeabi_dmul in our toolchain (arm-linux-gnueabi, libgcc) reveals multiple
data-dependent conditional branches (beq, bgt) associated with special-case handling (zero
operands, exponent normalization, denormalized numbers). Consequently, the constant-
time guarantee established in this work applies strictly to the core fixed-point Horner
evaluation, not to the end-to-end opt_expm function as currently implemented.
    A fully constant-time pipeline would require accepting the input x already in fixed-point
representation, thereby eliminating all floating-point operations and their associated soft-
float calls. This modification requires changing the calling convention of fpr_expm_p63
throughout the FALCON codebase and is identified as essential future work. We emphasize
this limitation explicitly: the present contribution demonstrates a constant-time polynomial
evaluation core, while achieving a fully isochronous fpr_expm_p63 remains open.

7.3    Precision versus Memory Trade-off
The ARM configuration (k = 16, d = 3, 256 B) achieves ≈ 2−28 precision, substantially
lower than both the x86-64 configuration (≈ 2−52 ) and the theoretical 2−63 target implied
by FALCON’s 63-bit output format. As established in Section 5, this precision reduction
does not weaken FALCON’s cryptographic security, which is independent of the Gaussian
sampler’s numerical precision beyond a very large statistical threshold (≈ 228 signatures
under one key). We nonetheless note that this trade-off was a deliberate design choice
favoring minimal memory footprint over maximal precision; Table 9 demonstrates that
higher-precision configurations (e.g., k = 64, 3584 B) remain available should a target
platform’s memory budget permit.

7.4    Comparison Scope
Our x86-64 results (Section 5) show performance parity rather than improvement relative
to the reference implementation, which itself already employs fixed-point arithmetic
with a degree-12 global polynomial (Section 2). This is an expected and informative
negative result: on architectures with fast native 64-bit or 128-bit integer multipliers,
our segmented approach does not significantly outperform an already carefully optimized
FACCT implementation.
    The primary performance contribution of this work therefore lies in constrained 32-bit
architectures (the FPU-less ARM configuration). Here it is essential to distinguish two

Why segmented degree-3 beats global degree-12. The effectiveness of segmentation
follows from the approximation error bound (Section 3): the error scales as wd+1 , where
w = ln 2/k is the segment width. Halving the interval width (doubling k) reduces the
error by a factor 2d+1 , permitting a substantial reduction in the polynomial degree at
constant precision. A global polynomial must span the entire interval [0, ln 2) with a
single approximation, forcing degree 12 in the FACCT reference and, on a 32-bit core, a
12-iteration loop of 96 executed multiplications (Section 6.4). Segmenting into 16 sub-
intervals lowers the per-segment requirement to degree 3, evaluated in only 12 unrolled
multiplications an 8× reduction at the cost of storing 16 coefficient sets (256 B versus
the reference’s 104 B) and one constant-time segment-selection step. Segmentation thus
trades arithmetic depth (costly and sequential on an FPU-less core) for table breadth
(cheap, constant-time, branchless). This trade is strongly favorable on the FPU-less IoT
targets addressed here, and unfavorable on a platform with native floating-point hardware
consistent with our x86-64 parity result (Section 5).

7.6      Future Work
We identify four directions for extending this work:

     1. Physical hardware validation. Repeating the speed and DUDECT measurements
        on a physical STM32F103 (Cortex-M3, no FPU) board, using an external timing
        harness (e.g., GPIO toggling captured by a logic analyzer) to eliminate QEMU-related
        measurement uncertainty.

     2. Energy measurement. Direct energy measurement on physical STM32F103
        hardware (via shunt resistor and oscilloscope) would quantify the energy impact of
        the reduced multiplication count. We deliberately avoid reporting an energy estimate
        derived from QEMU timings, as emulated execution time does not reflect physical
        Cortex-M3 cycle behavior (Section 5.6).

     3. Full fixed-point pipeline. Extending the approach beyond fpr_expm_p63 to other
        floating-point components of FALCON’s signing procedure, particularly the FFT-
        based Gaussian sampler tree, which represents a substantially larger optimization
        target than the single function studied here.

     4. Comparison with verification-side optimizations. Combining our signing-side
        optimization with existing ARM verification optimizations [CYS25] to provide a
        complete FPU-less FALCON implementation suitable for end-to-end IoT deployment.

     5. Fully constant-time argument reduction. Eliminating the residual soft-float
        calls (__aeabi_dmul, __aeabi_dsub) in the argument-reduction stage by accepting

8     Conclusion
This paper presented a systematic study of piecewise polynomial approximation applied to
fpr_expm_p63, the exponential evaluation function at the core of FALCON’s (FN-DSA,
FIPS 206) discrete Gaussian sampler. Combining the Remez minimax- algorithm, fixed-
point arithmetic, and constant-time Horner evaluation, we implemented and evaluated two
configurations: a 32-segment degree-6 approximation targeting x86-64, and a 16-segment
degree-3 approximation (256-byte LUT) targeting ARM Cortex-M3 microcontrollers with-
out hardware floating-point support.
    Our experimental results demonstrate that against the authentic FACCT reference from
Falcon’s fpr.c, our segmented Remez implementation achieves a 1.28× median speedup
on emulated ARM Cortex-M3 without FPU (range 1.24×–1.33× across 30 runs, variance
±3%), using a 256-byte LUT.
    Most significantly, our security analysis provides the first published empirical DUDECT
measurement of this function on emulated ARM Cortex-M3 against the authentic FACCT
reference. Both implementations satisfy the DUDECT statistical safety threshold in the
vast majority of runs (27/30 for our implementation, 30/30 for FACCT). Three marginal
outliers (t = 4.64, t = 5.09, and t = 5.24) are attributed to QEMU JIT scheduler
variance rather than genuine leakage an attribution supported by converging evidence from
instruction-level analysis, which confirms zero data-dependent conditional branches, zero
FPU instructions, and zero soft-float calls within the core Horner loop. This confirms a
branchless fixed-point Horner core, with the full constant-time claim appropriately limited
to the tested compilation target and memory model.
    These results directly address the concern raised by the NIST FIPS 206 standardization
forum regarding floating-point arithmetic in FALCON implementations, demonstrating
that a carefully constructed fixed-point alternative can match reference-implementation
performance on general-purpose hardware while providing measurable performance improve-
ments on FPU-less embedded targets precisely the class of devices for which FALCON’s
compact signatures are most attractive.
    We released our complete implementation, including the coefficient generation pipeline,
both target configurations, the DUDECT testing harness, and the QEMU-based ARM
benchmark infrastructure, to support reproducibility and to encourage further empirical
security analysis of FN-DSA’s reference implementation [FAL20] as it approaches final
standardization.
